newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: Russia firm against NATO expansion before summit.
newsitem.headline: Russia firm against NATO expansion before summit.

text.p: By Nicholas Doughty, Diplomatic Correspondent
A European security summit hoping to lay the foundations of peace for the 21st century opens on Monday, but with another row looming between Russia and the West over NATO expansion.

Leaders from the 54-nation Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) will approve plans for shoring up peace in Bosnia, set a new course for arms control and discuss problems such as the crisis in Belarus at the two-day summit.

Russian Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin, who met his Portuguese counterpart Antonio Guterres for talks after arriving in Lisbon, reiterated Moscow's tough line against plans by the Western alliance to take in new members from Eastern Europe.
"Russia is categorically against NATO expanding eastwards," he told reporters. "There is no need to rush."
"The fact that Europe is now without blocs is very important. We must work together. We must develop this, strengthen this," he added.
Russia says its security would be threatened if countries like Poland and Hungary join the Western alliance.

But Moscow has found little support for its efforts to develop the OSCE into a more powerful institution that would act as a counterbalance to NATO. It insists the summit must not appear to endorse the alliance's plans.
Western diplomats say they would prefer the Lisbon summit, which brings together the United States and Canada with European states, to avoid the debate on NATO enlargement.
The last OSCE summit two years ago in Budapest was wrecked by a row over the same issue and by differences over Bosnia.

As other leaders arrived in Lisbon for the meeting, a senior U.S. official told reporters Washington saw the OSCE and NATO as working together and said the summit was "not a debate about NATO enlargement".

Belarus President Alexander Lukashenko, facing international criticism after winning sweeping new powers in a controversial referendum last week, said that he believed the summit to be concerned mainly about NATO and European security.
"I must say it will be a very difficult summit because there will be very many disagreements concerning NATO and European states," he said before flying out of Minsk for Lisbon.
"Europe has been looking forward to becoming independent as far as its security is concerned. The United States and its supporters do not like that aim."
Leaders will issue a declaration in Lisbon committing them to develop a security blueprint for the continent.

"As we approach the new century, it is more important than ever that we build together a peaceful...region where all our nations and individuals feel secure," reads the declaration, a draft of which was obtained by Reuters.

Western nations, and Eastern European countries which are queuing up to join NATO, oppose any measures which would limit their freedom. The United States -- represented by Vice President Al Gore when he flies in from Washington for just a few hours on Monday -- has taken a tough line on this.
Diplomats said the summit declaration would endorse the general right of countries to join alliances, but without mentioning NATO so as to avoid any direct offence to Moscow.
Officials spent Sunday trying to reach final agreement on the summit documents, with debates on issues ranging from ethnic conflicts to arms control expected to last deep into the night.
One year after the end of the war in Bosnia, the meeting will agree a continued role for the OSCE there, working in parallel with the NATO-led peace force.

Leaders will also agree that a new round of arms talks should start in Vienna next year to reduce military hardware in Europe, adapting and expanding a 1990 treaty signed between NATO and the now-defunct Warsaw Pact.
